prompt: What is the name of the green pigment in chloroplasts that absorbs light energy?
hints: It's what makes leaves look green.
solution: **Chlorophyll** absorbs light energy, which the plant uses for photosynthesis. It absorbs red and blue light and reflects green light, which is why leaves look green.

prompt: Which gas do plants take in from the air for photosynthesis?

options.text: Carbon dioxide
Oxygen
Nitrogen
Hydrogen

feedback.b: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, so plants give it out. (They do use some oxygen for respiration.)
feedback.c: Nitrogen makes up most of the air, but plants can't use nitrogen gas directly.
feedback.d: There is almost no hydrogen gas in the air.

hints: It's the gas you breathe out more of.
solution: Plants take in **carbon dioxide** through their stomata. Photosynthesis turns carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

prompt: Which tissue carries water from the roots up to the leaves?

options.text: Xylem
Phloem
Epidermis
Palisade mesophyll

feedback.b: Phloem carries dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
feedback.c: The epidermis is the outer layer of cells that covers the leaf.
feedback.d: The palisade mesophyll is where most photosynthesis happens.

hints: It's made of long, hollow tubes of dead cells.
solution: **Xylem** carries water and dissolved minerals up from the roots to the leaves.

prompt: What are the tiny pores, mostly on the underside of a leaf, that let gases in and out?
hints: Each pore has a pair of guard cells around it.
solution: **Stomata** (one is a stoma). They let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out. Guard cells open and close them.

prompt: Complete the word equation for photosynthesis: [[a]] + water → [[b]] + oxygen
hints: One reactant comes from the air, through the stomata.
The product is the sugar that the plant makes first.
solution: **carbon dioxide** + water → **glucose** + oxygen. It needs light energy, absorbed by chlorophyll. The plant can turn the glucose into starch later, but glucose is made first.

prompt: Complete the word equation for respiration: glucose + [[a]] → carbon dioxide + [[b]] (+ energy released)
hints: Respiration is the reverse of photosynthesis.
solution: glucose + **oxygen** → carbon dioxide + **water** (+ energy released). It happens in the mitochondria of every living cell.

prompt: Match each part of a leaf to its job.

right.text: Air spaces let gases diffuse through the leaf
Brings water to the leaf cells

hints: The cuticle is a shiny, waterproof layer on top of the leaf.
Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts.
solution: Cuticle → reduces water loss. Palisade mesophyll → most photosynthesis. Spongy mesophyll → air spaces for gas diffusion. Guard cells → open and close stomata. Xylem → brings water.

prompt: What does phloem carry around a plant?

options.text: Dissolved sugars, from the leaves to other parts of the plant
Water and minerals, from the roots up to the leaves
Oxygen, from the leaves down to the roots
Starch grains, from the roots up to the leaves

feedback.b: That's the job of the xylem.
feedback.c: Gases move through a plant by diffusion through air spaces, not in the phloem.
feedback.d: Starch doesn't dissolve, so it can't be carried. Plants move sugars and turn them into starch where it is stored.

hints: Phloem moves the food that the leaves make.
solution: **Phloem** carries dissolved sugars made in the leaves to the parts of the plant that need them, such as roots, fruits and growing tips. It can carry them up or down.

prompt: When do plants carry out respiration?

options.text: All the time, day and night
Only at night, when it is dark
Only in the daytime, when it is light
Only on days when they can't photosynthesise

feedback.b: Plants respire at night, but they also respire during the day.
feedback.c: Respiration doesn't need light. Photosynthesis does.
feedback.d: Plants need energy all the time, so they respire all the time.

hints: Every living cell needs a constant supply of energy.
solution: Every living plant cell respires **all the time**, day and night, to release energy. In daylight, photosynthesis is usually faster than respiration, so overall the plant gives out oxygen. At night, it only respires, so it gives out carbon dioxide.

prompt: Select **all** the ways that leaves are adapted for photosynthesis.

options.text: A broad, flat shape
Thin, so gases don't have far to travel
Many chloroplasts near the upper surface
Stomata that let carbon dioxide in
A thick layer of bark covering the leaf
No air spaces, so the leaf is solid

hints: Think about what a leaf needs: light, carbon dioxide and water.
Gases need to diffuse through the leaf easily.
solution: A **broad, flat** shape gives a large surface area to absorb light. Being **thin** keeps diffusion distances short. **Chloroplasts near the top** catch the most light. **Stomata** let carbon dioxide in. Bark would block light. Leaves need air spaces so gases can diffuse to the cells.

prompt: Put these steps for testing a leaf for starch in the correct order.

items.text: Boil the leaf in water for about a minute
Put the leaf in hot ethanol (heated in a water bath, not over a flame) until it turns pale
Rinse the leaf in warm water to soften it
Spread the leaf on a white tile and add iodine solution
Look for a blue-black colour, which shows starch

hints: The chlorophyll has to be removed before you add iodine, or the green colour hides the result.
The ethanol step makes the leaf brittle, so it needs softening afterwards.
solution: 1. Boil in water (kills the cells and softens the leaf). 2. Hot ethanol in a water bath removes the chlorophyll. Ethanol is flammable, so never heat it over a flame. 3. Rinse in warm water to soften the brittle leaf. 4. Add iodine on a white tile. 5. Blue-black = starch; yellow-brown = no starch.

prompt: Water moves up the stem in the [[a]] and evaporates from the leaves through the stomata. This loss of water vapour from the leaves is called [[b]].
hints: One transport tissue carries water, and the other carries sugars.
solution: Water travels up the **xylem**. Its evaporation from the leaves is called **transpiration**, and it pulls more water up the xylem behind it.

prompt: Put these in order to show the path water takes through a plant.
hints: Water enters at the roots and leaves through the leaves.
It evaporates from the leaf cells into the air spaces before it escapes.
solution: Soil → root hair cell (by osmosis) → xylem in the root → xylem in the stem → mesophyll cell in the leaf → evaporates into an air space → diffuses out through a stoma (transpiration).

prompt: A variegated leaf has green parts and white parts. The white parts have no chlorophyll. After a sunny day, the leaf is tested for starch with iodine. What happens, and what does it show?

options.text: Only the green parts turn blue-black, showing chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis
The whole leaf turns blue-black, showing every part of a leaf photosynthesises
Only the white parts turn blue-black, showing that white parts store the starch
No part turns blue-black, because iodine only detects glucose

feedback.b: The white parts have no chlorophyll, so they can't photosynthesise and make starch.
feedback.c: The white parts can't photosynthesise, so they don't make starch.
feedback.d: Iodine detects starch, not glucose. Leaves store the glucose they make as starch.

hints: Which parts of the leaf can absorb light?
solution: Only the **green parts** have chlorophyll, so only they can photosynthesise and make starch. They turn blue-black, and the white parts stay yellow-brown. This shows that **chlorophyll is needed** for photosynthesis.

prompt: Plants change some of the glucose they make into an insoluble substance that can be stored. What is this substance?
hints: Kūmara and potatoes are full of it.
It turns iodine blue-black.
solution: **Starch**. It doesn't dissolve, so it is a good way to store glucose. It is stored in places such as kūmara roots, potato tubers and seeds.

prompt: Compare photosynthesis and respiration in a plant. Include the word equations, where in the cell each happens, when each happens, and what each does with energy.
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. It happens in the chloroplasts, so only in green cells, and only when there is light. It traps light energy and stores it in glucose. Respiration: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. It happens in the mitochondria of every living cell, all the time, day and night. It releases the energy stored in glucose so the cell can use it. The two reactions are opposites: the products of one are the reactants of the other.

rubric.criterion: Gives both word equations correctly (or clearly states that the products of one are the reactants of the other)
States where each happens: photosynthesis in chloroplasts, respiration in mitochondria (in all living cells)
States when each happens: photosynthesis only in light, respiration all the time
States that photosynthesis stores energy in glucose, while respiration releases energy from glucose

hints: Write the two word equations next to each other. What do you notice?
Which reaction needs light?
solution:
| | Photosynthesis | Respiration |
|---|---|---|
| Equation | carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen | glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water |
| Where | Chloroplasts (green cells) | Mitochondria (all living cells) |
| When | Only in light | All the time |
| Energy | Stores light energy in glucose | Releases energy from glucose |

prompt: Aroha shines a lamp on some pondweed in water and counts the bubbles it gives off each minute. When she moves the lamp closer, she counts more bubbles. What is the best conclusion?

options.text: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases
The bubbles are carbon dioxide, so the plant is respiring faster
The heat from the lamp is making the water boil, which makes bubbles
Pondweed can only photosynthesise when a lamp is very close to it

feedback.b: The bubbles are mostly oxygen, which is a product of photosynthesis.
feedback.c: The water is nowhere near boiling. A cool LED lamp, or a beaker of water between the lamp and the plant, stops the lamp warming the water.
feedback.d: Pondweed photosynthesises in any light, including sunlight. Brighter light just makes it faster.

hints: What gas is given off by photosynthesis?
What changes when the lamp moves closer?
solution: The bubbles are **oxygen** from photosynthesis. A closer lamp means **brighter light** (higher light intensity), and the plant gives off more oxygen, so the **rate of photosynthesis increases** as light intensity increases.

prompt: If an animal strips a complete ring of bark from around a tree's trunk, the tree usually dies. The phloem is just under the bark. Why does the tree die?

options.text: Sugars made in the leaves can't reach the roots, so the roots can't respire and they die
Water can't reach the leaves any more, because the xylem is in the bark
The leaves can't get carbon dioxide any more, because it enters through the bark
The roots can no longer make glucose to send up to the rest of the tree

feedback.b: The xylem is deeper, in the wood. Water can still travel up for a while, which is why the leaves stay green at first.
feedback.c: Carbon dioxide enters through the stomata in the leaves.
feedback.d: Roots don't photosynthesise. Glucose is made in the leaves.

hints: Where are sugars made, and which tissue carries them?
What do root cells need sugar for?
solution: Removing the bark removes the **phloem**. Sugars made in the leaves can no longer travel down to the roots. Without sugar, the root cells can't **respire**, so they die, and then the whole tree dies.

prompt: On hot, dry, windy days, many plants close their stomata. What is the main advantage and disadvantage of doing this?

options.text: It reduces water loss, but it also lets less carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis
It stops oxygen escaping, but it also stops the plant from respiring
It keeps heat out of the leaf, but it also blocks light from reaching the chloroplasts
It stops sugars leaking out, but it also stops water moving up the phloem

feedback.b: Plants don't need to keep oxygen in, and they can still respire using oxygen already inside the leaf.
feedback.c: Stomata don't control heat or light. Light passes through the transparent upper layers.
feedback.d: Sugars travel in the phloem, and water travels in the xylem. Neither leaks out through stomata.

hints: What escapes through open stomata?
What does the plant need to get in through its stomata?
solution: Closing the stomata **reduces water loss** by transpiration, which stops the plant wilting. But carbon dioxide also enters through the stomata, so **less carbon dioxide gets in** and photosynthesis slows down.

prompt: Palisade cells near the top of a leaf need carbon dioxide, water and light for photosynthesis. Explain how each one reaches them.
modelAnswer: Water is absorbed from the soil by root hair cells (by osmosis) and carried up the stem to the leaf in the xylem, inside the veins. Carbon dioxide diffuses from the air into the leaf through the stomata on the underside, then through the air spaces in the spongy layer to the palisade cells. Light passes through the transparent waxy cuticle and upper epidermis, and is absorbed by chlorophyll in the many chloroplasts in the palisade cells.

rubric.criterion: Water: absorbed by the roots and carried up to the leaf in the xylem
Carbon dioxide: diffuses into the leaf through the stomata and through the air spaces
Light: passes through the transparent upper layers and is absorbed by chlorophyll in the chloroplasts

hints: Take each one in turn: where does it start, and which part of the plant carries it?
Remember that the stomata are mostly on the underside of the leaf.
solution: Water: roots → xylem → leaf. Carbon dioxide: air → stomata → air spaces → palisade cells, by diffusion. Light: through the transparent upper layers → absorbed by chlorophyll.

prompt: Around dawn and dusk, there can be a time when a plant gives out no oxygen and takes in no carbon dioxide overall, even though it is still photosynthesising. Why?

options.text: Photosynthesis and respiration are happening at the same rate, so their gases cancel out
The plant stops all of its chemical reactions at dawn and at dusk
The plant has used up all the carbon dioxide inside its leaves
There is no light at all at dawn and dusk, so photosynthesis has stopped

feedback.b: Living cells never stop all their reactions. Respiration carries on all the time.
feedback.c: Carbon dioxide keeps being made by respiration, so it doesn't simply run out.
feedback.d: The question says the plant is still photosynthesising, so there must be some light.

hints: Two processes are going on in the plant. One uses carbon dioxide and the other makes it.
What happens if both go at exactly the same speed?
solution: In dim light, photosynthesis is slow. At one point it goes at **exactly the same rate as respiration**. The oxygen made by photosynthesis is all used by respiration, and the carbon dioxide made by respiration is all used by photosynthesis, so there is no overall gas exchange.

prompt: What type of energy do plants need for photosynthesis?
hints: Plants kept in a dark cupboard can't photosynthesise.
solution: Plants need **light energy**, usually from the Sun. It is absorbed by chlorophyll and stored as chemical energy in glucose.

prompt: Through which part of a plant does most of its water enter?

options.text: The roots
The leaves
The flowers
The bark of the stem

feedback.b: Water mostly **leaves** a plant through its leaves, by transpiration. It enters through the roots.
feedback.c: Flowers are for reproduction, not for taking in water.
feedback.d: Bark is a protective layer. Water enters through the roots, then travels up the stem in the xylem.

hints: Which part of the plant is in contact with damp soil?
solution: Water enters through the **roots**, mostly through root hair cells, which give a large surface area. It then travels up to the leaves in the xylem.

prompt: Which sugar do plants make by photosynthesis?
hints: It is the same sugar that your cells use for respiration.
solution: Photosynthesis makes **glucose**. Plants use it for respiration, turn it into starch for storage, or use it to build cellulose for cell walls.

prompt: [[a]] carries water and mineral ions up from the roots. [[b]] carries dissolved sugars from the leaves to the rest of the plant.
hints: One way to remember: **ph**loem carries **f**ood (sugars).
solution: **Xylem** carries water and mineral ions up from the roots. **Phloem** carries sugars made in the leaves to every part of the plant that needs them.

prompt: Select **all** the things a plant needs for photosynthesis.

options.text: Light
Carbon dioxide
Water
Chlorophyll
Oxygen
Soil
Glucose

hints: Think about the word equation for photosynthesis, and what absorbs the light.
solution: Photosynthesis needs **light**, **carbon dioxide**, **water** and **chlorophyll** (to absorb the light). Oxygen and glucose are its **products**. Soil isn't needed for photosynthesis: plants can even be grown in water with minerals dissolved in it.

prompt: What is the name of the pair of cells that open and close each stoma?
hints: They are bean-shaped cells in the lower epidermis, and they change shape to open or close the pore.
solution: Each stoma is surrounded by two **guard cells**. They change shape to open the stoma (letting gases in and out) or close it (to save water).

prompt: Which word equation shows photosynthesis?

options.text: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
carbon dioxide + oxygen → glucose + water
glucose + water → carbon dioxide + oxygen

feedback.b: This is **respiration**, the reverse of photosynthesis.
feedback.c: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis, not a reactant. The other reactant is water.
feedback.d: Glucose is **made** by photosynthesis, so it is a product, not a reactant.

hints: Photosynthesis uses a gas from the air and makes a sugar.
solution: Photosynthesis: **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen**, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. Respiration is the reverse.

prompt: Which variable must Tama keep the same, to make this a fair test?

options.text: The temperature of the water
The distance from the lamp
The number of bubbles per minute
The light intensity

feedback.b: This is the independent variable: Tama changes it on purpose.
feedback.c: This is the dependent variable: the result that Tama measures.
feedback.d: Tama changes the light intensity on purpose, by moving the lamp. It is what he is investigating.

hints: A controlled variable is something that could affect the results, but is not the thing being tested.
solution: The **temperature of the water** affects the rate of photosynthesis, so it must be kept the same. (A lamp can warm the water, so Tama could check it with a thermometer or use an LED lamp.) Distance and light intensity are what he's changing, and the bubbles are what he's measuring.

prompt: Describe the pattern in the results, and explain it.
modelAnswer: As the lamp was moved further away, the number of bubbles per minute decreased (from about 48 at 10 cm to 6 at 50 cm). The further away the lamp is, the lower the light intensity reaching the pondweed. With less light energy for the chlorophyll to absorb, photosynthesis happens more slowly, so less oxygen is made and fewer bubbles are given off.

rubric.criterion: Describes the pattern: as the distance increases, the number of bubbles per minute decreases
States that a lamp further away gives a lower light intensity at the pondweed
Explains that less light energy means a slower rate of photosynthesis, so less oxygen is produced

hints: First describe what happens to the bubble count as the distance increases.
Then link distance → light → rate of photosynthesis → oxygen.
solution: Further away → **less light** → **slower photosynthesis** → **less oxygen** → fewer bubbles.

prompt: A kauri seedling grows into a huge tree weighing many tonnes, but the soil around it hardly loses any mass. Where does most of the carbon in the tree's wood come from?

options.text: Carbon dioxide taken in from the air
Minerals taken in from the soil
Water taken in by the roots
Energy from sunlight

feedback.b: Minerals from the soil are important, but they make up only a tiny part of the tree's mass. That's why the soil hardly loses any mass.
feedback.c: Water is used in photosynthesis, but water contains no carbon.
feedback.d: Sunlight provides energy, not matter. Light can't add carbon atoms to the tree.

hints: Which of these contains carbon?
Think about the word equation for photosynthesis.
solution: In photosynthesis, the tree takes in **carbon dioxide from the air** and uses the carbon to make glucose, which is then built into cellulose and wood. Most of a tree's dry mass really does come from the air.

prompt: Why do most leaves look green?

options.text: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light, and reflects green light
Chlorophyll absorbs green light, which it uses for photosynthesis
Leaves are full of green sap, which fills the cell vacuoles
Green light is the only colour of light that plants can use

feedback.b: We see the colours that are **reflected**, not the ones that are absorbed. Chlorophyll absorbs very little green light, so it bounces back to our eyes.
feedback.c: Cell sap is mostly clear. The green colour comes from chlorophyll in the chloroplasts.
feedback.d: Plants use mostly red and blue light. Green is the colour they use least.

hints: When you see something as a certain colour, is that colour being absorbed or reflected?
solution: Chlorophyll absorbs mainly **red and blue** light for photosynthesis and **reflects green** light. The reflected green light reaches our eyes, so leaves look green.

prompt: Put these in order to show the path a carbon dioxide molecule takes from the air to a chloroplast in a palisade cell.

items.text: A stoma on the underside of the leaf
An air space in the spongy mesophyll
The cell wall and cell membrane of a palisade cell
A chloroplast inside the palisade cell

hints: Gases enter a leaf through pores, mostly on its lower surface.
The spongy layer has spaces that let gases move through the leaf.
solution: Air → **stoma** → **air spaces** in the spongy mesophyll → into the **palisade cell** (through its wall and membrane) → **chloroplast**. It moves all the way by diffusion.

prompt: Before testing a leaf for starch, students often keep the plant in a dark cupboard for two days. Explain why.
modelAnswer: In the dark, the plant can't photosynthesise, so it can't make any new glucose or starch. It keeps respiring, and it uses up or moves away the starch already stored in its leaves. This 'destarches' the leaves, so if starch is found later in the experiment, you know it was made during the experiment and wasn't already there.

rubric.criterion: Explains that in the dark there is no photosynthesis, so the plant uses up or moves away the starch already in its leaves
Explains that any starch found later must have been made during the experiment (so the result is valid)

hints: What can't a plant do in the dark?
Why would it matter if starch was already in the leaf at the start?
solution: Two days in the dark **removes the starch** that was already in the leaves (no photosynthesis, but respiration continues). Then any starch found later **must have been made during the experiment**.

prompt: Most of the chloroplasts are in layer B. Why is this layer near the **top** of the leaf?

options.text: It gets the most light, which chloroplasts need for photosynthesis
It is closest to the stomata, where carbon dioxide enters
It is closest to the vein, which brings glucose into the leaf
It is protected from the wind, which damages chloroplasts

feedback.b: Most stomata are on the **lower** surface of the leaf, a long way from layer B.
feedback.c: The vein brings **water**. Glucose is made in the leaf, and the phloem carries it away.
feedback.d: Wind is not the reason. Light comes from above, so the top layer gets the most.

hints: Where does the light come from?
solution: Light shines on the top of the leaf, so the **top layer gets the most light**. Packing the chloroplasts there means they can absorb as much light as possible for photosynthesis.

prompt: Most stomata, like D, are on the lower surface of a leaf. What is the main advantage of this?

options.text: Less water is lost, because the lower surface is shaded and cooler
More light can reach the stomata on the lower surface
Rain cannot get in through the stomata and drown the cells
Carbon dioxide is heavy, so it collects underneath leaves

feedback.b: The lower surface gets **less** light, and stomata don't need light to let gases in.
feedback.c: Rain is not the problem. The main issue for a leaf is **losing** too much water.
feedback.d: Carbon dioxide mixes evenly in the air around a leaf. The real advantage is about saving water.

hints: Water vapour escapes through open stomata.
Which surface of the leaf is out of the direct sun?
solution: Water vapour escapes through open stomata. The lower surface is out of direct sunlight, so it is **cooler** and **less water evaporates**. With most stomata underneath, the leaf can still take in carbon dioxide while losing less water.

prompt: Compare xylem and phloem. Include what each one carries, the direction it carries it, and what each is made of.
modelAnswer: Xylem carries water and dissolved mineral ions, while phloem carries dissolved sugars (made in the leaves). Xylem carries its contents in one direction only, up from the roots to the leaves; phloem carries sugars both up and down, to wherever they are needed, such as the roots, growing tips, fruit and seeds. Xylem is made of dead cells that form hollow tubes with strong, thickened walls; phloem is made of living cells.

rubric.criterion: States that xylem carries water and mineral ions, and phloem carries dissolved sugars
States that xylem carries upwards only (roots to leaves), while phloem carries both up and down to where sugars are needed
States that xylem is hollow tubes of dead cells (with strong walls), while phloem is made of living cells

hints: Remember: phloem carries food (sugars).
Where are sugars needed? Are those places all above the leaves?
solution:
| | Xylem | Phloem |
|---|---|---|
| Carries | Water and mineral ions | Dissolved sugars |
| Direction | Up only (roots → leaves) | Up and down (to where sugar is needed) |
| Made of | Dead cells forming hollow tubes with strong walls | Living cells |

prompt: Kauri dieback is caused by a fungus-like microbe that lives in soil. It infects the roots and damages the tissues that carry water and nutrients inside the tree. Infected trees often have yellowing leaves and a thinning canopy. Why do the leaves suffer, when it is the roots that are infected?

options.text: Damaged roots and transport tissues can't supply the leaves with enough water and minerals
The microbe travels up into the leaves, where it destroys the chlorophyll
The disease blocks the stomata, so carbon dioxide can't get into the leaves
The roots can't photosynthesise any more, so no glucose reaches the leaves

feedback.b: The disease attacks the roots and the base of the trunk. The leaves suffer because they are cut off from water and nutrients.
feedback.c: The disease does not block the stomata. The problem is the supply from the roots.
feedback.d: Roots don't photosynthesise. Glucose is made in the leaves and carried **down** to the roots.

hints: What do the leaves need from the roots?
Which tissue carries it up the trunk?
solution: Leaves need **water** and **mineral ions** from the roots. When the roots and the tissues that carry water up the trunk are damaged, the leaves don't get enough, so they turn yellow and the canopy thins. Over time, the whole tree can die.

| Amount of CO₂ | Colour |
|---|---|
| Less than in normal air | Purple |

Riya sets up three sealed tubes of red indicator. In tubes A and B, a leaf is held above the indicator on a small mesh platform. After a few hours:

- **Tube A** (leaf, bright light): the indicator turned **purple**.
- **Tube B** (leaf, tube wrapped in foil so it is dark): the indicator turned **yellow**.
- **Tube C** (no leaf, bright light): the indicator stayed **red**.
prompt: Why did the indicator in tube B turn yellow?

options.text: In the dark, the leaf only respired, which added carbon dioxide
In the dark, the leaf photosynthesised, which added carbon dioxide
The foil reacted with the indicator and turned it yellow
The leaf stopped all of its life processes in the dark

feedback.b: Photosynthesis needs light, and it **uses up** carbon dioxide. It doesn't add it.
feedback.c: The foil was wrapped around the outside of the tube to block the light. It didn't touch the indicator.
feedback.d: Living cells respire all the time, day and night.

hints: Which process can a leaf carry out in the dark?
Yellow means more carbon dioxide than normal.
solution: Yellow means **more** CO₂. In the dark, the leaf can't photosynthesise, but it still **respires**, releasing carbon dioxide into the tube.

prompt: Lena paints clear nail varnish on the underside of a leaf, peels it off and looks at it under a microscope. She counts 36 stomata in an area of 0.2 mm². The underside of the leaf has an area of 20 cm². Estimate the total number of stomata on the underside of the leaf. (1 cm² = 100 mm²)
hints: First work out how many stomata there are in 1 mm².
Then convert the leaf's area into mm² and multiply.
solution:
Stomata per mm²: $36 \div 0.2 = 180$.

Leaf area: $20 \text{ cm}^2 = 20 \times 100 = 2000$ mm².

Total: $180 \times 2000 = 360\,000$ stomata.

prompt: A small plant sealed inside a glass jar with some damp soil, on a sunny windowsill, can stay alive for months. An animal, such as a snail, sealed in a jar on its own would soon die. Explain the difference.
modelAnswer: In the light, the plant photosynthesises: it takes in carbon dioxide and water and makes glucose (its food) and oxygen. The plant also respires all the time, using oxygen and glucose and releasing carbon dioxide. Over each day, photosynthesis makes enough glucose and oxygen to cover what respiration uses, and the carbon dioxide from respiration is reused for photosynthesis, so the gases are recycled inside the jar. The snail can only respire: it uses up the oxygen and food and builds up carbon dioxide, and it has no way of turning carbon dioxide back into oxygen or making more food, so it soon dies.

rubric.criterion: States that the plant photosynthesises in the light, making its own food (glucose) and oxygen from carbon dioxide and water
Explains that the plant's respiration uses oxygen and releases carbon dioxide, which photosynthesis reuses, so the gases are recycled
Explains that the animal only respires: it uses up the oxygen (and food) and builds up carbon dioxide, which it can't turn back into oxygen

hints: Which processes does the plant carry out? Which does the snail carry out?
Think about what each process uses up and what it makes.
solution: The plant **photosynthesises and respires**, so oxygen and carbon dioxide are recycled and it makes its own food. The snail **only respires**, so it uses up the oxygen and food with no way to replace them.

prompt: Most leaves have most of their stomata on the lower surface. Water lilies have leaves that float flat on the surface of a pond, and their stomata are on the **upper** surface. Why?

options.text: The lower surface lies on the water, so gases from the air can only get in through the top
The upper surface gets more light, which the stomata need so they can photosynthesise
Carbon dioxide enters from the pond water, so the lower surface needs no stomata
Stomata on the upper surface trap bubbles of air that help the leaf to float

feedback.b: Stomata are pores that let gases in and out. They are on top so they can reach the air, not so they can photosynthesise.
feedback.c: Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air through their stomata. Stomata on the underside would be covered by water.
feedback.d: Floating comes from air spaces inside the leaf and stem, not from the stomata.

hints: Stomata let carbon dioxide in from the air.
Which surface of a floating leaf is touching the air?
solution: Stomata let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out. A water lily's lower surface lies on the water, so stomata there would be blocked. Its upper surface is in the air, so that is where the stomata are. Saving water isn't a problem for a plant growing in a pond.
